title: Ig Nobel Prize hunt

metric.name: loss
metric.label: interesting-finding loss
metric.description: 1 - score: unconfirmed or group-targeting studies score 0; otherwise score = 0.25 + 0.75 * committee score (lower judge's min(laugh, think)/10). With IGNOBEL_COMMITTEE=off (explicit gate-only scoring), confirmed studies score 1.0; otherwise the committee requires TINKER_API_KEY.

brief: a pre-registered study by a domain expert (`prereg.json`, a JSON object; no code runs). Each agent is an expert in one field (descriptor mechanism = field, method = study_type) and must do real research first: read papers via the swarm's Exa leads, then register BEFORE seeing data: {field, study_type, question, hypothesis, mechanism (why the effect should exist), citations (>= 2 Exa source ids S<k> or URLs from this run's research, or sources.json), dataset: {url of a real public CSV/TSV (open-data host such as raw.githubusercontent.com, zenodo, figshare, OSF, Dryad, data.gov, Rdatasets, or a URL in the Exa results), x, x_level, y, y_level (exact column header text; level = the answer compared vs everyone else, omit for numeric columns)}, direction (positive|negative), predicted_rho (expected |Spearman rho|)}. The host verifies citations, downloads the data once, and runs the registered test ONCE on all rows (Spearman, p < 0.005 and |rho| >= 0.1 in the registered direction; one test per dataset per run, so a second registration on a used dataset scores 0). Trivial pairs (same column, near-identical wording, two demographics) score 0. Significant means p < 0.005 and |rho| >= 0.1 in the registered direction on all rows; split-half consistent means the same registered direction, |rho| >= 0.1, and p < 0.05 in each of the two fixed hash halves. Unconfirmed studies score 0. Confirmed studies score 0.25 + 0.75 * committee score (the lower judge's min(laugh, think)/10); a targets_group rejection gives score 0. Loss = 1 - score. Only with the explicit IGNOBEL_COMMITTEE=off opt-out (gate-only scoring, used for fake-LLM runs) do confirmed studies use score 1.0; otherwise the committee requires TINKER_API_KEY. Before judging, the host searches the host-written headline once with Exa when enabled and sends up to five title/URL/snippet results; established or textbook relationships must receive THINK <= 3. Judges see only the host-written abstract and prior-work results, never your question, hypothesis, or mechanism. If a column name is wrong the run fails and lists the dataset's usable columns. The baseline registration (rare-steak eaters smoke more) is a real hypothesis that fails (loss 1); aim for an interesting, funny and thoughtful non-obvious finding that shows split-half consistency. Labs are open-ended: field may be any snake_case field or subfield you found (myrmecology, psychoacoustics, ...), not only the listed ones; a new subfield is logged as descriptor other/<subfield>. Each round the task inputs add the lab notebook (every study registered so far this run and its result: build on other labs' ideas and nulls, never repeat a tested dataset) and real downloadable datasets found on Zenodo and Hugging Face with their column names. When two labs report the same finding (same dataset, same column pair), only the earliest counts. Derived rates: dataset.x_per / dataset.y_per may name a numeric denominator column, so a numeric variable is tested per unit of another (e.g. "Bites" per "Minutes observed"); the host computes the rate itself.

fake_edits.idea: Register fruity candies lose FiveThirtyEight candy matchups

replace_with.question: Do fruity candies lose head-to-head popularity contests against non-fruity candies?
replace_with.hypothesis: Candies flagged fruity win a smaller share of FiveThirtyEight's pairwise candy matchups.
replace_with.mechanism: Chocolate is the most craved and liked sweet (Rozin et al. 1991; trait chocolate craving predicts implicit chocolate preference), and fruity candies are mostly non-chocolate, so they should lose most pairwise votes.

fake_edits.idea: Register parents find babies on planes less rude

replace_with.question: Do parents of minors judge bringing a baby on a plane as less rude than non-parents?
replace_with.hypothesis: Respondents with children under 18 more often answer that bringing a baby on a plane is not at all rude.
replace_with.mechanism: Parents perceive infant cries as less aversive and more interpretable than non-parents do (Green & Gustafson 1986; Green, Jones & Gustafson 1987), so a crying baby in the cabin should seem less of a breach of etiquette to them.

dataset.x: Do you have any children under 18?
dataset.y: In general, is itrude to bring a baby on a plane?

proxy_note: pre-registered confirmatory test on real public data; committee-scored in-run, with cached verdicts reported by score_run.py

scout.goal: a real, odd, everyday phenomenon (human, animal, food or object behaviour) that is documented in published research or open data the swarm has NOT used yet, ideally with a downloadable raw CSV/TSV
scout.channels: paper_query: search papers and past Ig Nobel winners for a measurable everyday oddity. code_query: search for a raw, downloadable CSV/TSV dataset on that oddity (GitHub raw files, Zenodo, figshare, OSF, Dryad, data.gov).
scout.pick_criterion: points to real data (ideally a direct CSV/TSV URL) or a real published effect the study can test on the existing surveys
scout.extract_question: Give any direct CSV/TSV download URL for the data, what each column measures, and the sample size.
